Since releasing pplx-embed-v1 in February, we have been working on a new generation of embedding models. Last week, we introduced our new contextual embedding model, pplx-embed-v2-context . Today, weâre expanding the family with pplx-embed-v2-late , a collection of late-interaction models. Alongside stronger retrieval capabilities, the models are the first to combine three core features:

- Multi-vector representations . Rather than compressing each input into a single vector, these models retain token-level vectors for finer-grained query-document comparisons. This allows different parts of a query to match different parts of a document, preserving detail that is especially valuable for multimodal retrieval.

- Support for both text and image modalities . In addition to the text-to-text retrieval capabilities of our previous models, these new models handle text-to-image retrieval, allowing them to directly search rendered PDF pages without requiring OCR or parsed text.

- A shared embedding space . We are releasing two model sizes, 0.6B and 9B, to support different quality, latency, and compute requirements. Each can be used independently, but the shared embedding space also allows the smaller model to query an index created with the larger model, combining higher-quality document embeddings with cheap, fast query-time inference.

These new models achieve state-of-the-art results on a range of vision and text retrieval benchmarks, as well as agentic question-answering tasks. Notably, on ViDoRe (V3) , a leading visual document retrieval benchmark, our 0.6B model matches models with five times as many active parameters. Both models are publicly available on Hugging Face .

## From single vectors to late interaction

Retrieval systems must find a balance between efficiency and the depth of interaction between queries and documents. Dense embedding models encode each query and document independently, allowing them to be compared with a cheap inner product. This makes approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search over billions of documents practical. At the other extreme, cross-encoders process the query and document together, enabling richer interaction but requiring a separate forward pass for every candidate. Applying this computation across a large corpus of documents for every search is prohibitively expensive, so cross-encoders are typically reserved for reranking a small set of retrieved candidates.

### Limitations of dense embeddings

Representing an entire document with one fixed-size vector creates an information bottleneck. As documents grow longer and cover more topics, the model must compress more content into the same vector, making it harder to preserve everything relevant to a query. Chunking can reduce this pressure, but it fragments the document and can separate information that only makes sense together, an issue we also tackle with our contextual embedding model . This bottleneck worsens in multimodal settings, where the information density of images requires even more compression.

Single-vector dense retrieval also reduces every comparison to an inner product between two vectors, limiting the expressivity of the scoring function. For a fixed embedding dimension and a large enough corpus, some patterns of scores across query-document pairs are impossible to produce, regardless of training. The LIMIT benchmark turns this theoretical concern into a concrete stress test for single-vector retrieval.

### Late-interaction retrieval

Late-interaction models occupy the space between the cheaper dense embedding models and the more expressive cross-encoders. Like dense models, they encode documents independently of the query, allowing document representations to be computed offline. However, rather than reducing each input to a single vector, they retain multiple vectors and use a richer scoring function when comparing a query with a document.

Our pplx-embed-v2-late models use a ColBERT-style architecture, outputting 128-dimensional embeddings for each token in the input. We score query-document pairs using MaxSim; for each query token, the model selects the highest-scoring document token and sums the per-token maximum similarities to produce the final score. This lets different parts of a query match different parts of a document, with stronger token matches contributing more to the score.

This additional expressiveness comes with higher storage and candidate-scoring costs. Dense retrieval stores one vector per document and scores a candidate with one inner product; late interaction stores vectors for document tokens and evaluates many token-to-token similarities. The cost grows with document length, so late interaction requires a different indexing and serving trade-off than one-vector ANN retrieval. In return, it provides richer first-stage retrieval for quality-sensitive corpora and can also serve as a later stage in a larger web-scale retrieval pipeline.

## One model, multiple modalities

This improved depth of interaction has been shown to be very useful for various tasks, including long-context, agentic and out-of-domain retrieval. This difference is particularly evident in multimodal retrieval, as shown by the large lead of ColPali models on the ViDoRe(V3) leaderboard.

Real-world corpora are not composed only of clean text. They arrive as PDFs, slide decks, screenshots, scanned pages, charts, and tables. The conventional pipeline parses these documents, applies OCR or captioning, and searches the resulting text, which is expensive and lossy: it can introduce OCR errors and it discards layout, table structure, figures, and spatial relationships. Visual document search skips that step, projecting the rendered page directly into the representation space where textual queries can search it.

Our new family of models builds on the strong performance of multi-vector models for multi-modal search and advances the Pareto frontier for small models on the most widely used document search benchmark, ViDoRe(V3). While we expect document renderings to be the most common form of visual input, our models also support semantic image search over natural images, such as scenic photographs.

## Training a family of interoperable models

Search is fundamentally asymmetric: indexing and query encoding have different operational constraints. Indexing runs offline and can be parallelized, so its compute cost is amortized across many future searches. Query encoding runs online for every request, making it latency-sensitive and sometimes subject to serving or edge-device limits. Our model family makes use of this asymmetry, offering sizes tailored to each side of the retrieval pipeline.

We train an 18B teacher contrastively, then distill it separately into 9B and 0.6B students. Rather than training each student only to reproduce the teacherâs ranking distribution, we use LEAF -style representation distillation: for each input token, we align the studentâs output embedding with the teacherâs. While representation-space distillation has previously been used for dense, single-vector models, we extend it to late interaction, where the alignment target is a vector for every retained token.

As a result, both released checkpoints share the same multi-vector embedding space. This enables cross-model retrieval, making additional deployment options possible.

- Maximum quality: encode documents and queries with the 9B model.

- Maximum efficiency: encode documents and queries with the 0.6B model for 100% local inference

- Low-latency retrieval: build the corpus index with the 9B model, then encode live queries with the 0.6B model to leverage index-time computation while keeping querying fast.

- Localâcloud retrieval: encode private local documents or live queries with the 0.6B model on-device, and compare or merge those representations with results from a 9B index hosted in the cloud.

For latency-sensitive settings, we designed the 0.6B model as a lightweight query encoder that can also run on edge devices. Starting from Qwen3.5-0.8B , we prune its 24-layer text tower to 12 layers, reducing that tower from 498M to 240M non-embedding parameters. The resulting model has 594M parameters in total, but its nominal size overstates the serving cost: 100M are used for image encoding, and 254M sit in the token-embedding table, which has little effect on runtime. Only about 240M parameters are active for text encoding and 340M for image encoding, giving the model the serving cost of a substantially smaller model while retaining compatibility with the 9B index.

We applied the same process to build our 18B teacher from a 27B backbone, which made the teacher considerably cheaper to distill from without weakening the signal it provides.

### Multilingual, multimodal, uncontaminated training data

We train both models on a dataset of 186 million query-document pairs drawn from 594 datasets in 46 languages. Of these pairs, 88.3% are text-to-text, 8.3% are text-to-image, and 3.4% are text-to-visual-document pairs. Rather than sampling in proportion to dataset size, we assign each dataset a sampling weight, which yields a more balanced training mixture of 56.5%, 30.9%, and 12.6%, respectively.

When constructing our training data, we exclude any datasets associated with benchmarks that we evaluate on to faithfully represent our results without inflating benchmark scores. This decision comes with the trade-off that some of the datasets we chose to exclude contain high-quality data which could improve the performance of our model on tasks besides the benchmark they came from. Ultimately, we chose to accept that cost: trustworthy numbers are more useful to us during development, and to users when comparing models.

## Evaluation

We evaluate both models across text, visual-document, mixed-image, and agentic retrieval. Both models outperform the evaluated baselines on Q2D-Web and BrowseComp+, and achieve strong results on visual-document retrieval and MADQA.

### Text retrieval

We evaluate text-to-text retrieval on three benchmarks:

- Domain-specific benchmarks : A collection of 72 MTEB-style tasks, 55 across five domains (finance, legal, health, conversation, tech), plus 17 miscellaneous multilingual tasks. The collection includes tasks such as FinQA, AILACasedocs and XLSum. None of these datasets appear in our training data, as described above.

- Q2D-Web : our web-scale retrieval benchmark of about 70,000 agent-reformulated search queries, drawn from production search traffic, over a corpus of 190M web documents. This benchmark measures retrieval performance in a setting much closer to real-world web retrieval than other available retrieval benchmarks, due to its production-like queries and large-scale corpus.

- ViDoRe(V3) Markdown : ViDoRe(V3) is typically a text-to-visual-document retrieval task, but it can also be evaluated as a text task using a version of the corpus that has been parsed to Markdown, allowing us to evaluate information-rich document retrieval in both image and text modalities.

We measure performance using nDCG@10, except on Q2D-Web, where we report Recall@1000 due to the benchmarkâs focus on a first-stage web-retrieval scenario. Throughout our evaluations, we compare against industry-leading embedding models across different size classes. For text retrieval, nemotron-embed-8b , gemini-embedding-2 , voyage-large-4 , and qwen3-embed-8b represent the strongest and most widely used dense competitors, while voyage-4-nano and qwen3-embed-0.6b serve as sub-billion parameter dense baselines. We additionally compare against TopK's recently released topk-embed-v1 late-interaction models on the benchmarks for which TopK has published results. ViDoRe(V3) scores are taken from their model cards at 128 dimensions, matching the width of our token embeddings; the Q2D-Web score is taken from our leaderboard.
